hook.support: Think of a brand you know. You know its colours. You know how it talks. You know what it stands for. Now make your own.
hook.core: Close your eyes and picture a brand you love. You can probably see its colours, hear how it talks, and say what it stands for. That’s not luck. Every part was chosen to send one clear message. This is the Advocate boss mission: you’ll build a brand of your own.
hook.extend: A brand is a promise, kept the same everywhere. A name, a look, a voice and a set of values all send one message to one audience. Building one draws on this whole zone. You’ll use language for an audience, visual cues, platform features and evaluation.

why.support: Brands are everywhere. Making one shows you how they work.
why.core: Small businesses, clubs, bands and causes all need a brand. Knowing how to build one, and why it works, is a real skill.
why.extend: Branding mixes writing, design and planning. It’s key to marketing, small business and community work. It also sharpens how you read every brand around you.

articles.title: More than a logo

body.support:
A **brand** is more than a **logo**. It is the whole feel of a business, group or person.

**Start with one message.** What do you want people to think and feel? Say it in one sentence.

**Make a brand kit:**
- **Name:** short and easy to say.
- **Logo:** a simple picture or design.
- **Colours:** two or three, used every time.
- **Slogan:** a short, catchy line.
- **Brand voice:** how your brand talks. Funny? Calm? Bold?
.
**Be consistent.** Use the same colours and voice every time. Then people will know it’s you.

**Think about your audience.** Bright colours and jokes might suit kids. Calm colours might suit a health clinic.

**Test it.** Show people. Ask what they think it stands for. If they get it wrong, fix it.
body.core:
A **brand** is the whole personality of a business, group or person: its name, look, voice and **values**. A good brand sends one clear message, everywhere it appears.

**1. Start with the message and audience.**
- Who is it for? Be specific: “young skaters in our town”, not “everyone”.
- What should they feel and remember? Write it in one sentence.
.
**2. Build the brand kit.**
- **Name:** short, easy to say and spell, and fits the feeling.
- **Logo:** simple enough to draw from memory; works in black and white.
- **Colours:** two or three. Colours send messages: green for nature, red for energy, blue for trust.
- **Slogan:** short and catchy. Rhythm, rhyme or a twist help.
- **Brand voice:** how the brand talks. Is it cheeky, calm, bold or caring?
.
**3. Make it consistent.** Every poster, post and sign should use the same colours and voice. Consistency builds trust and makes the brand easy to recognise.

**4. Create the material.** Posts, a poster, a label or a webpage, all carrying the same message.

**5. Test, revise and edit.** Show it to your audience. Ask: what does this brand stand for? Who is it for? Would you buy or join? Fix what they didn’t get. Edit spelling and punctuation last.
body.extend:
A **brand** is the sum of the choices that make a business, group or person recognisable: name, visual identity, voice and **values**. Strong brands are **consistent**. Every touchpoint reinforces the same message for the same **target audience**.

**Strategy first.**
- **audience:** a specific group, with needs and values you can name.
- **message:** what the brand should make them think and feel, in one sentence.
- **values:** what the brand stands for, such as sustainability, fun, fairness or quality.

**Identity.**
- **name:** memorable, pronounceable, and suited to the message.
- **logo:** simple, scalable, recognisable in one colour.
- **colour and type:** colours carry associations (green with nature, blue with trust, orange with energy); fonts carry tone.
- **slogan:** compressed message, often using rhythm, rhyme or wordplay.

**Voice.** A **brand voice** sets word choice, sentence length, humour and formality. A **brand guide** records these rules, so anyone can create on-brand material.

**Material.** A brand comes alive across a set of texts: social posts, a poster, packaging, a webpage. Each uses its platform’s features but stays consistent in message, look and voice.

**Evaluate and revise.** Test with the target audience. Can they say what the brand stands for, and who it’s for? Revise strategy and identity first, then edit the copy.

caseStudies.title: The man on the toilet

body.support:
In **2012**, three friends in **Melbourne** started a business. It sold **toilet paper**.

They called it **Who Gives A Crap**. The name was cheeky. It made people laugh.

They needed money to start. So one of them, **Simon Griffiths**, sat on a toilet in a warehouse. He said he would not get up until people had ordered **$50,000** of toilet paper.

It was streamed live online. He sat there for **50 hours**. Then they reached their goal.

The company says it gives half its profits to help build toilets in poor countries.

The name, the stunt and the cause all sent one message: funny, but doing good.
body.core:
In **July 2012**, three friends in **Melbourne** launched a toilet paper company. They gave it a name you don’t forget: **Who Gives A Crap**.

To raise money to start, co-founder **Simon Griffiths** sat on a toilet in an empty warehouse. It was streamed live online. He promised not to get up until people had ordered **$50,000** of toilet paper.

He sat there for **50 hours**. The campaign hit its target, and the first rolls were delivered in 2013.

The company says it gives half its profits to help build toilets in poorer countries.

Everything about the brand matches. A cheeky name. A stunt that made people laugh. Bright paper wrappers. And a serious cause underneath. It is **funny on the outside, doing good on the inside**.
body.extend:
In **July 2012**, three Melbourne friends launched **Who Gives A Crap**, a toilet paper company with a social mission. Co-founder **Simon Griffiths** raised the start-up money with a stunt: he sat on a toilet in an empty warehouse, streamed live, and promised not to stand until the crowdfunding campaign reached **$50,000** in pre-orders.

He stayed for **50 hours**, and the target was met. The first product shipped in 2013. In 2021, CNBC reported the company had raised $30 million from investors.

The company says it donates 50% of its profits to sanitation charities.

The brand is a study in consistency. The name is irreverent. The launch stunt was absurd but memorable. The packaging is bright and playful. The voice is cheeky, and the mission is serious. Each choice reinforces one message for one audience: people who want everyday shopping to do some good, without being lectured.

It shows that humour and a serious cause can sit inside one brand, as long as every piece points the same way.

teacher.overview: The Advocate boss mission. Students design a brand for themselves, a product or a community group: one message, a specific audience, and a brand kit (name, logo, colours, slogan, voice), then three consistent posts. They test it with their audience, revise and edit. The case study is Who Gives A Crap (Melbourne, 2012), whose cheeky name, 50-hour toilet-sitting launch stunt and serious sanitation cause all point the same way.
prep: Coloured pencils or devices for logos and posts.
Collect a few strong local brands (cafés, clubs) to discuss.
Students should have done Brand You, Why Ads Work or One Message first; this mission draws on all three.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 one-sentence message; 2 specific audience; 3 simple logo; 4 colours for energy and street style; 5 short slogan with rhythm; 6 consistent voice; 7 values.

**Sort:** on brand — “snapped your deck”; slogan with orange and black; “local kid, local shop”. Off brand — formal trading-hours notice; pastel pink and gold; “only losers…” (rude, not cheeky).

**Case study:** Griffiths sat on a toilet for 50 hours, streamed live, until $50,000 in pre-orders came in (July 2012); the cheeky name, funny stunt, playful wrappers and serious cause all send one message: funny on the outside, doing good inside.

resources.label: CNBC — the CEO who sat on a toilet for 50 hours (2021)

realityCheck: **The brand name includes “crap”.** It’s mild and it’s the real name, but check it suits your school community.
**Logo design can stall students who “can’t draw”.** Stress simple shapes; free design tools are fine.
**Personal brands:** some students prefer a product or club. Offer all options.
**Works in a real class:** yes. The “on brand or off brand” sort makes consistency obvious, and students enjoy testing posts on each other.

levels.support: Aimed at about Years 3–4 reading: shorter article and case study, 6 key words, word bank, brand kit frame and two posts.
levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with message, audience, brand kit, three posts and testing.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: brand strategy, values, a brand guide, purposeful posts and evidence-based evaluation.
